papers.title: Predicting cerebrospinal fluid α-synuclein seed amplification assay positivity in borderline hyposmia.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) α-synuclein seed amplification assays (SAAs) provide valuable biomarkers of underlying α-synuclein pathology. Although more severe olfactory impairment is associated with a higher likelihood of CSF α-syn SAA positivity in prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD), a simple tool to enrich candidates for CSF biomarker testing is lacking, particularly among individuals with borderline hyposmia. We aimed to develop and internally validate an exploratory clinical prediction model for CSF α-syn SAA positivity in this subgroup. METHODS: A total of 83 participants with age- and sex-adjusted University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) percentiles >15 and ≤ 20 were included from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) Phase 2 prodromal cohort. A prediction model was developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression with 16 candidate predictors and 10-fold cross-validation. Internal validation was performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples repeating the complete model-development procedure. RESULTS: Among 83 participants, 43 (51.8%) were SAA-positive and 40 (48.2%) were SAA-negative. The LASSO model retained age, sex, REM Sleep Behavior Disorder Screening Questionnaire (RBDSQ) score, and Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) score. The apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.927, and the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.896, with an optimism-corrected Brier score of 0.149. CONCLUSION: This exploratory four-variable LASSO model demonstrated promising discrimination for CSF α-syn SAA positivity among individuals with borderline hyposmia. External validation in larger, independent cohorts is required before clinical application.

papers.title: Dissociable noradrenergic and cholinergic contributions to cognitive function in early Parkinson's disease: A free-water imaging study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To distinguish the roles of the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC) and cholinergic systems (nucleus basalis of Meynert [NBM], pedunculopontine nucleus [PPN]) in early Parkinson's disease (PD) cognitive impairment using free-water imaging (FWf). METHODS: FWf metrics were derived from the LC and cholinergic pathways via probabilistic tractography in 114 de novo PD patients from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative. Cross-sectional, linear mixed-effects, and Cox models assessed associations with cognition and progression to cognitive/functional decline over 5 years. RESULTS: Cross-sectionally, LC integrity specifically linked to visuospatial function (BJLO), while NBM lateral pathway integrity uniquely associated with processing speed (SDMT). LC showed stronger associations with HVLT immediate recall, NBM with HVLT discrimination. Longitudinally, baseline LC FWf predicted declines in semantic fluency (β = -0.124, P = 0.016) and immediate verbal recall (β = -0.131, P = 0.007); NBM lateral FWf predicted decline in verbal discrimination (β = -0.078, P = 0.021). NBM lateral FWf independently predicted onset of cognitive impairment (HR = 1.72, 95% CI:1.07-2.77, P = 0.026) and functional decline (HR = 2.57, P = 0.021). Conventional DTI metrics (MD, AD, RD) in the NBM lateral pathway consistently predicted both endpoints. CONCLUSIONS: LC-noradrenergic and NBM-cholinergic systems show dissociable cognitive contributions in early PD: LC integrity broadly associates with multiple domains cross-sectionally, whereas cholinergic pathway integrity-especially NBM lateral projections-emerges as a robust predictor of future cognitive and functional decline.

papers.title: Squalamine prevents motor and non-motor symptoms in the paraquat and lectin rat model of the body-first subtype of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Increasing evidence supports the existence of a distinct body-first subtype of Parkinson's disease (PD), in which the initial site of pathology is in the gut. Animal models that recapitulate the body-first subtype of PD are needed. We tested the hypothesis that non-motor features of the body-first subtype of PD are recapitulated in the paraquat and lectin (P + L) rat model of PD, a model that has previously demonstrated the pathological motor progression of this subtype of PD. Then, we tested whether oral squalamine, a gastrointestinal prokinetic that has been shown to reduce formation of pathological α-synuclein, could prevent pathology, motor, and non-motor findings. Rats (n = 93) were orally gavaged for seven days with paraquat (1 mg/kg) and lectin (0.05%) in 1% sucrose solution. A subset of rats (n = 37) were given 30 days of squalamine (20 mg/kg) in their drinking water immediately following P + L treatment. papers.title: Discontinuation and optimization of device-aided therapies in Parkinson's disease: a prospective comparative real-world study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Comparative real-world evidence on device-aided therapy (DAT) persistence in Parkinson's disease (PD) is limited. We assessed discontinuation, reasons, optimization time, and associated factors. METHODS: We analyzed the prospective multicenter DATs-PD GETM Spanish Registry (January 2024-May 2026), including deep brain stimulation (DBS), continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI), foslevodopa/foscarbidopa (fLD/fCD), levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), and levodopa-entacapone-carbidopa intestinal gel (LECIG). Persistence and associated factors were examined using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses. RESULTS: Among 565 patients receiving 591 DATs, 170 (28.8%) treatments were discontinued: DBS 4.1% (4/97), CSAI 34.1% (45/132), fLD/fCD 34.7% (101/291), LCIG 28.6% (4/14), and LECIG 28.1% (16/57). Among infusion therapies, discontinuation was 33.6%, without significant differences in rates (p = 0.774) or Kaplan-Meier persistence (p = 0.701). Main reasons were adverse events (38.2%) and patient decision (25.3%). Mean optimization time was 61.6 ± 97.2 days (LECIG 19.6 ± 33.1; DBS 115.2 ± 118.3). Discontinuation was associated with institutional caregiving (HR 5.162, 95% CI 1.441-18.490), higher ON-state Hoehn and Yahr stage (HR 1.814, 95% CI 1.110-2.964), and longer daily OFF time (HR 1.093, 95% CI 1.002-1.193). CONCLUSIONS: Approximately one-third of infusion DATs were discontinued, with no significant persistence differences. Disease severity, OFF time, and caregiving environment were associated with discontinuation. Observational differences in selection and exposure preclude direct comparative-effectiveness conclusions.

papers.title: LPC (18:1) Modulates Seeded α-Synuclein Aggregation and Associated Cellular Toxicity in a Stable HEK293FT Model.
papers.abstract: Synucleinopathies are characterized by pathological α-synuclein (α-Syn) aggregation. Our research group previously developed and marketed Porcine Liver Decomposition Product (PLDP) as a functional supplement, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study evaluated the effects of LPC (18:1), a constituent of PLDP, on seeded α-Syn aggregation and associated cellular stress responses using a newly established HEK293FT model. A stable α-Syn-expressing HEK293FT cell line, selected for its high sensitivity to exogenous α-Syn fibril seeds, was utilized. In vitro assays showed that LPC (18:1) inhibited α-Syn fibril elongation. In the cellular model, treatment with LPC (18:1) in the micromolar range attenuated seed-induced intracellular α-Syn aggregation, reduced phosphorylated α-Syn (Ser129) accumulation, restored cell viability, and suppressed LDH release. Furthermore, LPC (18:1) reduced intracellular ROS generation and down-regulated the mRNA and protein expression of inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and IL-1β). These findings indicate that LPC (18:1) modulates seeded α-Syn aggregation and associated toxicity and cytokine responses in an engineered HEK293FT model. They do not establish neuroprotective or anti-inflammatory effects in disease-relevant cells, therapeutic efficacy, or the effects of PLDP as a formulation.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation is an early pathological process in a mouse model of prodromal Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Approximately 90% of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients exhibit olfactory deficits, which often precedes motor symptoms by years, and are a robust predictor for PD and subsequent cognitive decline. Pathological changes in the PD olfactory system, particularly α-synuclein (αSyn) pathology in the olfactory bulb (OB) and severe involvement of the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), are distinct from normal aging. However, the causal link between αSyn aggregation and functional impairment, potentially involving cytotoxicity and neuroinflammation, remains elusive. To investigate these early pathological events, we utilized a prodromal PD model that we have previously characterized, involving the unilateral OB injection of αSyn pre-formed fibrils (PFF) in wild-type mice. This triggers the transneuronal spread of pathogenic αSyn, and olfactory dysfunction starting at 1-month post-injections. Here we report on neuropathological and inflammatory events 1-3 month following injection of PFFs into the OB. Following PFF injection, αSyn pSer129 pathology progressively accumulated bilaterally in the AON and ipsilateral in the piriform cortex (PCX) over three months. Stereological quantification revealed no significant neuronal loss in the AON or PCX during this 1-3 month interval, indicating that olfactory impairment precedes overt neurodegeneration. papers.title: Disrupted cortical signatures of response inhibition in Parkinson's disease revealed by TMS-EEG.
papers.journal: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Inhibitory control deficits are a hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD), particularly in patients with L-DOPA-induced dyskinesias (LID), but the cortical mechanisms underlying impaired inhibition remain poorly understood. We used transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) to investigate cortical dynamics during a Go/NoGo task in PD patients with and without LID, compared with healthy volunteers. METHODS: Thirty-six PD patients (18 LID-PD, 18 nLID-PD) and 20 healthy volunteers performed a Go/NoGo task during TMS-EEG, which assessed functional connectivity between the supplementary motor area (SMA) and primary motor cortex (M1), and cortical reactivity through TMS-evoked potentials. RESULTS: Healthy volunteers exhibited task-dependent modulation of SMA-M1 connectivity, with increased theta-band coupling during NoGo trials and gamma-band coupling during Go trials; this pattern was absent in both PD groups, particularly in those with dyskinesias. TMS-evoked potentials revealed enhanced N100 responses during NoGo trials in healthy volunteers, reduced in non-dyskinetic patients and absent in dyskinetic ones. SMA-M1 gamma connectivity correlated with motor performance and clinical severity. During post-TMS epochs, healthy volunteers showed context-dependent alpha/beta modulation that was disrupted in PD patients. CONCLUSIONS: SMA-M1 communication and cortical inhibitory processing are impaired in PD, especially in patients with dyskinesias. SIGNIFICANCE: SMA dysfunction may represent a biomarker and therapeutic target for inhibitory deficits in PD.

papers.title: The CheckBRAIN™ platform: architecture for post-screening brain health care across the Parkinson's disease continuum.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) screening can identify people needing clinical assessment but does not itself provide continuing care. Drawing on Thailand's smartphone-based CheckPD implementation and selected literature, this conceptual review proposes CheckBRAIN, a platform linking screening to personalised brain-health care. All CheckPD participants would be offered voluntary entry, while clinician-led assessment would proceed without delay when clinically indicated. Concerning screening results, new or progressive symptoms, clinically defined high-risk syndromes, diagnostic uncertainty or medication-related problems would trigger clinical review, while people with established PD could enter directly. A personal brain-health portfolio links multidomain functioning, systemic and environmental context, priorities, actions, responsible persons or services and review dates. The six-domain SHAPES framework supports priority setting without creating another diagnostic score. Actions may include diagnostic assessment, medication review or pharmacotherapy, rehabilitation, cue-linked daily habits, social support, and service-level responses to practical barriers such as transport, digital access, referral navigation or unavailable services. Primary-care teams would coordinate longitudinal review, community workers would support assisted or non-digital participation, and specialists would contribute according to clinical need. Intended benefits include understandable next steps, fewer unresolved referrals, support for everyday function and participation, and clearly defined roles for care partners with the participant's consent. We outline staged co-design and evaluation of feasibility, safety, functioning, participation, caregiver burden, equity, service use and costs. CheckBRAIN is not intended as a population registry and has no fixed national enrolment target. It remains a proposed care architecture, not a validated intervention or evidence of PD prevention or cost saving. It

papers.title: Cause, Situation, and Impact of Nonaccidental Falls in Persons with Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease - A Hospital-based Patient-Perceived Observational Study.
papers.abstract: Clinical characteristics, drug responsiveness, and natural history of Parkinson's disease are different in India compared to the Western world. This hospital-based descriptive study was conducted, as anecdotal information alone is available on the characteristics of falls in idiopathic Parkinson's disease from India. To collect the data of characteristics of falls, a structured interview was conducted in 192 consecutive idiopathic Parkinson's patients with a history of minimum three falls in the previous 3 months and normal cognition. The mean duration and severity of the disease were 5.3 ± 3.29 and 3.42 ± 0.58, respectively. Majority of the falls are caused by disease-related impairments, postural instability (50.7%, 1085) and freezing (32.5%, 694), during walking (42.42%, 907), turning (21.18%, 453), and getting up (32.08%, 686). Fourteen (7.3%) participants sustained fracture and 30.7% (59) of participants required medical intervention costing ₹200-₹200000/. Quality of life as measured by the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (31.19 ± 13.36) was positively correlated with number of falls ( r = 0.38, P = 0.000). Falls have a considerable impact on the patients and caregiver.

papers.title: PIKfyve inhibition induces LRRK2 activation through phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate and CASM.
papers.abstract: LRRK2 is a Parkinson's disease-associated kinase that phosphorylates Rab GTPases. Hyperactivation of LRRK2, which is thought to cause Parkinson's disease, occurs on stressed endolysosomal membranes via conjugation of ATG8 to single membranes (CASM) and Rab, whereas the involvement of specific membrane lipids remained unclear. Here, we found that the inhibition of PIKfyve that metabolizes phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) induces hyperactivation of LRRK2 and that additional inhibition of the class III phosphoinositide 3-kinase that generates PI3P suppressed LRRK2 hyperactivation. Cellular PI3P levels were indeed elevated when LRRK2 was activated. CASM-induced activation of LRRK2, but not CASM itself, was suppressed by phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitors, whereas inhibition of CASM or Rab12/Rab29 suppressed LRRK2 activation induced by PIKfyve inhibitors. LRRK2 and phospho-Rab10 were colocalized with PI3P on LAMP1-positive enlarged vacuoles, and LRRK2 directly bound PI3P in vitro via its N-terminal positively charged amino acids. Together, we propose an updated mechanism of LRRK2 hyperactivation that simultaneously requires CASM, Rab, and PI3P-rich membranes.
